title: Kinematics in One, Two, and Three Dimensions
short_intro: Kinematics is the branch of classical mechanics that describes the motion of points, bodies, and systems without consideration of the masses or the forces acting on them. It relies on the mathematical description of position, displacement, velocity, and acceleration as functions of time.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Uniform and uniformly accelerated motion in one and two dimensions, equations of motion, relative velocity, and projectile motion under constant gravitational acceleration.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: General curvilinear motion in polar and cylindrical coordinate systems, velocity and acceleration in rotating frames, Coriolis and centrifugal accelerations, and motion under central forces.

prerequisites: Vector algebra (addition, dot product, cross product, and derivatives of vectors)
Calculus (differentiation and integration of single and multivariable functions)
Fundamental concepts of coordinate systems (Cartesian, polar, and cylindrical)

concept_notes.heading: Displacement, Velocity, and Acceleration
bullets: Displacement vector r(t) defines the position of a particle relative to an origin O.
Instantaneous velocity is the time derivative of the position vector: v = dr/dt.
Instantaneous acceleration is the time derivative of the velocity vector: a = dv/dt = d2r/dt2.

concept_notes.heading: Motion with Constant Acceleration
bullets: When acceleration a is constant, vector equations decouple into orthogonal Cartesian components.
The velocity increases linearly with time: v(t) = v0 + at.

concept_notes.heading: Projectile Motion
bullets: Motion in a uniform gravitational field is analyzed by separating horizontal and vertical components.
Horizontal acceleration is zero, maintaining a constant horizontal velocity component (if air resistance is neglected).
Vertical motion is governed by constant downward gravitational acceleration g.

concept_notes.heading: Kinematics in Polar Coordinates
bullets: For planar motion, position is given by r = r r̂.
Velocity vector has radial and transverse components: v = ṙ r̂ + r θ̇ θ̂.
Acceleration vector includes centripetal and Coriolis-type inertial terms: a = (r̈ - rθ̇2) r̂ + (rθ̈ + 2ṙθ̇) θ̂.

derivations.title: Equation of Path for a Projectile
derivations.conditions: Uniform gravitational field, launch angle θ<sub>0</sub> from origin (0,0), neglect air resistance
steps: Write parametric equations for horizontal and vertical positions as functions of time: x = v<sub>0</sub>cos(θ<sub>0</sub>)t and y = v<sub>0</sub>sin(θ<sub>0</sub>)t - (1/2)gt<sup>2</sup>.
Express time t from the horizontal motion equation: t = x / (v<sub>0</sub>cos(θ<sub>0</sub>)).

Substitute the expression for t into the vertical position equation: y = v<sub>0</sub>sin(θ<sub>0</sub>)[x / (v<sub>0</sub>cos(θ<sub>0</sub>))] - (1/2)g[x / (v<sub>0</sub>cos(θ<sub>0</sub>))]<sup>2</sup>.
Simplify the trigonometric terms to obtain the parabolic trajectory equation.

derivations.title: Acceleration Components in Polar Coordinates
derivations.conditions: Planar motion in polar coordinates (r, θ)
steps: Define unit vectors in polar coordinates: r̂ = cos(θ)î + sin(θ)ĵ and θ̂ = -sin(θ)î + cos(θ)ĵ.
Differentiate unit vectors with respect to time: dr̂/dt = θ̇ θ̂ and dθ̂/dt = -θ̇ r̂.
Write velocity vector as v = d(r r̂)/dt = ṙ r̂ + r(dr̂/dt) = ṙ r̂ + rθ̇ θ̂.
Differentiate the velocity vector with respect to time to obtain acceleration: a = d/dt(ṙ r̂ + rθ̇ θ̂).
Substitute time derivatives of unit vectors and group terms into radial (r̂) and transverse (θ̂) components.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Displacement-Time (s-t) Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A curved line sloping upwards with increasing slope on a Cartesian plane with t on x-axis and s on y-axis.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The slope of the tangent at any point on the s-t graph represents the instantaneous velocity of the particle.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Direct questions calculating velocity from curve slopes or identifying stationary vs moving states.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Velocity-Time (v-t) Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A straight line with a positive constant slope starting from a non-zero intercept on the v-axis.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The slope of the v-t graph gives acceleration, and the area under the curve represents total displacement.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Extensively used to find displacement under varying acceleration and to derive kinematic equations graphically.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Acceleration-Time (a-t) Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A horizontal straight line parallel to the time axis for uniform acceleration.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The area under the a-t graph over a given time interval represents the change in velocity (Δv).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Testing cumulative velocity changes when acceleration is a function of time.

solved_numericals.question: A particle moves along a straight line with an initial velocity of 5 m/s and a constant acceleration of 2 m/s<sup>2</sup>. Find its displacement and final velocity after 4 seconds.
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: u = 5 m/s, a = 2 m/s<sup>2</sup>, t = 4 s.
Use displacement formula: s = ut + (1/2)at<sup>2</sup>. Substitute values: s = (5)(4) + (1/2)(2)(4)<sup>2</sup>.
Use velocity formula: v = u + at. Substitute values: v = 5 + (2)(4) = 13 m/s.

solved_numericals.question: The position of a particle moving in a plane is given by r(t) = 3t2î + 4t2ĵ. Find the magnitude of its total acceleration at t = 2 s.
solution_steps: Differentiate position vector to find velocity: v(t) = dr/dt = (6t)î + (8t)ĵ.
Differentiate velocity vector to find acceleration: a(t) = dv/dt = 6î + 8ĵ.
Observe that acceleration is independent of time and constant: a = 6î + 8ĵ m/s2.
Calculate the magnitude of acceleration: |a| = √(62 + 82) = √(36 + 64) = √100 = 10 m/s2.

solved_numericals.question: A projectile is fired with an initial velocity of 20 m/s at an angle of 30° to the horizontal. Calculate the maximum height reached. (Take g = 10 m/s<sup>2</sup>)
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: v<sub>0</sub> = 20 m/s, θ<sub>0</sub> = 30°, g = 10 m/s<sup>2</sup>.
Recall the formula for maximum height: H = (v<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup> sin<sup>2</sup>θ<sub>0</sub>) / (2g).
Substitute values into the formula: H = [(20)<sup>2</sup> × 0.25] / (2 × 10) = [400 × 0.25] / 20 = 100 / 20 = 5 m.

assumptions_and_limitations: Macroscopic point-mass approximation: Objects are treated as point particles, ignoring rotational kinematics about their internal center of mass unless explicitly specified.
Galilean relativity: Kinematic equations assume inertial reference frames unless fictitious forces (e.g., centrifugal, Coriolis) are explicitly incorporated for non-inertial frames.

common_misconceptions.wrong: At the maximum height of a projectile, both velocity and acceleration are zero.
common_misconceptions.correct: At maximum height, only the vertical component of velocity is zero; the horizontal velocity remains non-zero, and acceleration is still constant downward equal to g.
common_misconceptions.why: Gravity acts continuously throughout the flight, and horizontal motion has no opposing force in the absence of air resistance.

common_misconceptions.wrong: If the speed of a particle is constant, its acceleration must be zero.
common_misconceptions.correct: A particle moving at constant speed in a curved path experiences non-zero centripetal acceleration.
common_misconceptions.why: Acceleration is the rate of change of the velocity vector, which includes changes in direction as well as magnitude.

quick_revision: Velocity is the time derivative of position; acceleration is the time derivative of velocity.
In projectile motion, horizontal velocity remains constant while vertical motion is under uniform acceleration g.
Polar acceleration includes both centripetal (rθ̇<sup>2</sup>) and Coriolis (2ṙθ̇) components.
